questions.text: When does the work after await Promise.resolve() run inside an async function?
options: As a microtask, after the current synchronous code
Immediately, on the same line
As a macrotask with setTimeout(0)
Only on the next requestAnimationFrame

questions.text: Two Promise.then callbacks queued together run before the next setTimeout(0).
What happens if a microtask enqueues another microtask?
questions.answer: The new microtask joins the same queue and still runs in this drain, before any macrotask. The queue is emptied completely, so a then/queueMicrotask chain can delay timers.

questions.text: Relative to the promise microtask queue, process.nextTick in Node.js is…
options: An even higher-priority queue than promise microtasks
The same as setTimeout(0)
Identical to browser queueMicrotask with no differences
A macrotask after all timers

questions.text: An async function runs synchronously until its first await.
Why does a nested setTimeout(0) inside then not run right after that then?
questions.answer: then is a microtask. setTimeout enqueues a macrotask. The event loop finishes every current microtask first, then takes the timer. So the nested timeout always waits for the next macro turn.

What does calling an async function return?
options: A promise: return fulfills it, throw rejects it
The raw return value, with no promise
undefined until the function reaches an await
A setTimeout macrotask

questions.text: Which statement about awaiting an already fulfilled promise is true?
options: The code after await runs immediately because the promise is already fulfilled
The code after await is still deferred to microtasks
await turns the continuation into a setTimeout(0)
await waits for the next requestAnimationFrame

questions.text: queueMicrotask and Promise.then queued one after another from synchronous code run…
options: then always before queueMicrotask
queueMicrotask as a macrotask, then as a microtask
On one microtask queue, in the order they were queued
Alternating with timers: one microtask, one timer

questions.text: What does .catch do?
options: It turns a rejection into a macrotask
It runs the callback synchronously if the promise is already rejected
It pauses the event loop until the error is handled
It queues a rejection handler as a microtask, like then

questions.text: When does fn in Promise.all(...).then(fn) start if every input fulfills?
options: As a microtask after the last input fulfills
Synchronously, as soon as every promise is created
As a separate macrotask per input
Only if some input rejects

questions.text: Why does then return a new promise?
options: To stop the microtask queue
So the next then can follow the result of this callback
To turn the chain into one macrotask
No new promise is created: then mutates the original

questions.text: If then returns a plain number, the next then…
options: Receives that number synchronously, before the current callback ends
Is queued as a setTimeout
Receives that number as its own microtask, with no promise to unwrap
Does not run: then only accepts promises

questions.text: Two async functions called one after another, before their awaits…
options: The second does not start until the first finishes entirely
Their post-await continuations alternate with setTimeout
The first runs completely, including code after await, and only then the second
Both run their synchronous start, and only then do the continuations after await

questions.text: How is await 0 different from synchronous code on the next line?
options: 0 is wrapped in a fulfilled promise, and the continuation still goes to microtasks
await 0 stays synchronous because 0 is not a promise
await 0 becomes a setTimeout(0)
Awaiting a number throws TypeError

options: undefined, and no promise
A promise that fulfills with undefined when the function finishes
A promise appears only if the function contains await
A rejected promise

questions.text: A finally callback, relative to the then on that same step…
options: Runs synchronously at the end of then
Is a macrotask
Is also a microtask and runs after that then callback
Runs before then

questions.text: A throw before the first await inside an async function looks like this to the caller…
options: A synchronous exception at the call
The script stops on that line
An error that an outer try/catch around the call always catches synchronously
A rejection of the returned promise, delivered asynchronously

questions.text: In what order do queueMicrotask callbacks queued in a synchronous for loop run?
options: In iteration order, all as microtasks after the loop
In reverse order
As separate setTimeout tasks
The first one runs while the loop is still going

options: Yes, if resolve is called synchronously
No: then is still a microtask

questions.text: await stops all other JavaScript until the promise fulfills.
.catch on an already rejected promise runs synchronously.
In a .then().then() chain, the second callback is queued before the first one runs.
On success, Promise.all waits for every input promise before running its then.
finally is skipped when the promise already has a then.
Two queueMicrotask callbacks queued one after another from synchronous code do not overtake each other.
A setTimeout queued inside a microtask can run before microtasks that were already queued.
then on the promise returned by an async function with no await still runs as a microtask.
An exception inside then rejects the promise that then returned.
The then of Promise.race runs synchronously when race is called.
Code after await runs in the same stack turn as the code before await.
A plain, non-async function called from then runs synchronously inside that then.
A queueMicrotask from synchronous code runs before a setTimeout(0) that was queued on the line above.
If an async function throws, the promise it returned is rejected.
Why doesn’t the second then in a chain start before the first one finishes?
questions.answer: The second callback follows the promise returned by the first then. Until that callback settles, there is nothing for the second to react to, so it is queued only afterward.

questions.text: How is await different from then for the surrounding function?
questions.answer: await pauses that async function and returns control to the caller. The continuation after await is a microtask. then does not pause the function that called it: the callback is only queued.

questions.text: What is an unhandled promise rejection?
questions.answer: A rejection that nobody attached a catch to. It is delivered asynchronously, so a try/catch around the async call does not catch it.

questions.text: How does a successful Promise.all relate to microtasks?
questions.answer: Each input settles through its own reaction. The then on all is queued as a microtask when the last input fulfills, not when all is called.

questions.text: Why doesn’t await 0 continue on the next line?
questions.answer: 0 is not a promise, but await wraps it in a fulfilled promise and still defers the continuation to microtasks.

questions.text: When does process.nextTick from synchronous code run ahead of Promise.then in Node.js?
questions.answer: When both are queued from ordinary synchronous code, Node drains the nextTick queue before promise microtasks. nextTick is Node’s own queue, separate from then.

questions.text: Can a setTimeout(0) that is already queued slip between two thens of one chain?
questions.answer: No. While microtasks keep queueing microtasks, the macrotask waits. The timer starts only after the microtask queue is empty.

questions.text: What happens on a throw inside then?
questions.answer: The promise returned by that then is rejected. A later catch also runs as a microtask. The surrounding synchronous code has already finished.

questions.text: How far do two async functions called one after another run synchronously?
questions.answer: Each one runs until its own first await. Both synchronous starts finish before any continuation after await.

questions.text: Is finally a separate queue?
questions.answer: No. It is a microtask for the promise’s settlement, both fulfillment and rejection. It does not jump ahead of microtasks already queued.

questions.text: Why can code after an async call run before the code after await inside that function?
questions.answer: The call only runs until await and returns a promise. The caller continues. The rest of the function waits for its microtask.

questions.text: What does .catch do when the promise fulfills?
questions.answer: The catch callback is not called. The chain stays fulfilled: a following then receives the promise’s value.

questions.text: Why doesn’t resolve() in the executor call then on the same line?
questions.answer: resolve only fulfills the promise. then reactions are separate microtasks, and they start after the current stack.

questions.text: Why does then return a new promise instead of the same one?
questions.answer: So the next step waits for this callback, not for the original promise. Otherwise chain subscribers would be mixed with listeners of the start.
